titulo: The Apparatus That Outlives the Regimes
subtitulo: The interwar years, the Metaxas dictatorship, and the repressive machinery every subsequent government would inherit (1923–1940)

coda.heading: October 28, 1940, and the coda for the trip
intro: In the early hours of October 28, 1940, the Italian ambassador delivered Metaxas an ultimatum demanding free passage of Italian troops through Greek territory. Metaxas rejected it. Tradition condenses the reply into a single word, OCHI, "no," and October 28 has since been a national holiday, "No Day." The Italian army invaded from Albania, was halted in the mountains of Epirus, and counterattacked: within a few weeks the Greeks occupied a quarter of Albania. It was the Axis's first land defeat of the war, and it had an enormous moral effect on a Europe that had known nothing but capitulations.

items.text: The paradox is among the most uncomfortable in Greek history, and it is worth stating without resolving it: the hero of the founding act of national antifascist resistance was a dictator who governed with censorship, internment camps, and a political police, and whose regime had borrowed the aesthetics of the very regimes it was now fighting. Metaxas died in January 1941, before the German invasion in April. Greek national memory preserves October 28 and keeps a relative silence about August 4. That a country celebrates as a national holiday an act by a dictator is a fact about how memories function: they select episodes, not biographies.

closing: For the trip: in Athens, note the flags and the parades if you coincide with a commemoration, and observe which dates have a street or a square and which do not. In Corfu, the old and new fortresses, with the history of the three bombardments. And a useful question to raise, if the trust arises: what families tell about the occupation. It is the subject of the next installment, which covers the darkest period — famine, resistance, the extermination of Corfu's Jewish community in 1944 — and in which your island destination stops being peripheral and becomes central stage.

sections.heading: A republic without republicans
paragraphs: The defeat of 1922 destroyed the monarchy's legitimacy, since it had ordered the final offensive. Six officers and politicians of the royalist government — among them a former prime minister and the commander-in-chief — were summarily tried and shot in November 1922, in the episode known as the Trial of the Six, which poisoned the Schism even further. The republic was proclaimed in 1924.

The eleven years that followed are a catalogue of instability: more than twenty governments, some dozen coups or attempted coups, alternating purges of the army and administration depending on which faction of the Schism held power. Venizelos governed again between 1928 and 1932 with a public-works program — drainage, schools, roads — and with a remarkable diplomatic turn: in 1930 he signed a friendship agreement with Turkey that formally renounced all territorial claims, and he even went so far as to nominate Mustafa Kemal for the Nobel Peace Prize. The man who had embodied the Megali Idea signed its death certificate. It is one of the most remarkable acts of political realism of the European interwar period, and it cost him much of his base.

Then came the world crisis. The 1929 collapse sank exports — tobacco and raisins — and cut off remittances from Greek emigrants in the United States, which had been a crucial source of foreign currency. In 1932, Greece suspended payments for the second time in forty years and abandoned the gold standard. Venizelos fell, and with him the last possibility of republican stabilization.

sections.heading: 1935–1936: the restoration and the coup
paragraphs: After a failed Venizelist attempt in March 1935, the royalist army thoroughly purged the officer corps. That November a plebiscite on the monarchy was held whose results — around ninety-seven percent in favor of restoration — were acknowledged as fraudulent even by its beneficiaries. King George II returned.

The elections of January 1936 left a parliament without a majority, with fifteen Communist deputies holding the balance between the two blocs of the Schism. In April, the king appointed as prime minister Ioannis Metaxas, a royalist general whose party had won only seven seats. And on August 4, 1936, on the pretext of a general strike called by the unions, Metaxas suspended key articles of the constitution, dissolved parliament, and established a dictatorship, with the king's signature and support.

The REGIME OF THE FOURTH OF AUGUST presented itself as the Third Hellenic Civilization — after the ancient and the Byzantine — with a compulsory youth organization, prior censorship, exaltation of the peasantry and the army, and an aesthetic borrowed from Italian fascism without its mass base or its single party. Metaxas never had a movement: he had the king, the army, and the police. It is what the literature calls a conservative dictatorship rather than a fascism proper, and the distinction matters because it explains how it functioned: it sought not to mobilize society but to demobilize it.

The anecdote usually cited is telling: censorship banned performances of Sophocles's Antigone and even expurgated Pericles's funeral oration as dangerous. A regime that grounded its legitimacy in continuity with ancient Greece, censoring ancient Greece. The contradiction is not comic: it is the structural trait of all authoritarian nationalisms, which need a glorious, sterilized past, from which grandeur is extracted and content is eliminated.

sections.heading: The finding: the apparatus that outlives the regimes
paragraphs: This is the most important argument of this installment and probably one of the most transferable in the whole plan.

Metaxas's minister of public security, Konstantinos Maniadakis, built between 1936 and 1940 a machinery of surveillance and political repression of remarkable efficiency: systematic infiltration of the Communist Party — to the point of controlling its internal apparatus and publishing a fake party newspaper — files on militants, mass arrests, deportation to confinement islands such as Anafi, Folegandros, or Gavdos, and the practice of DECLARATIONS OF REPENTANCE, public recantation documents demanded of detainees and kept on file.

Now observe what happens next. Metaxas dies in January 1941 and his regime dissolves with the German invasion. But the files, the personnel, the confinement islands, the procedure of the declaration of repentance, and the legal framework against communism do not disappear: they are inherited and expanded by the Greek state after 1945, used massively during the civil war and afterward — with the camps at Makronisos and Gyaros — maintained throughout the postwar period through the so-called certificate of national convictions, required to obtain public employment, a driver's license, or a passport, and put back into operation by the colonels in 1967 with the same lists and sometimes the same officials. The files were not destroyed until 1989, by a reconciliation law, and their burning was a political event.

The analytical conclusion: regimes change, THE APPARATUS REMAINS. A democracy that inherits intact the repressive machinery of a dictatorship is not simply a democracy with an uncomfortable past: it is a democracy that keeps, available and operational, the capacity to do it again, and that also retains within itself the personnel trained to do so.

The Peruvian application is direct and needs no embellishment. The intelligence and control apparatus built during the internal armed conflict, the practices of filing social leaders and organizations, the figure of terruqueo as a mechanism of political exclusion, and the continuity of personnel and institutions across governments of opposite sign, are the same structure. The debate over police reform that Peru has been postponing for twenty years is, at bottom, this same debate: it is not about the conduct of individuals but about which institutional capacities are retained, and for what purpose. Greece took fifty-three years to burn its files, and it did so through an explicit political pact, not through natural evolution.

sections.heading: The simultaneous world: Peru in the 1930s
paragraphs: The simultaneity with Peru in these years is strikingly precise. In 1930 Leguía falls after eleven years of personalist government, swept away by the world crisis that sank export prices and closed off North American credit; Peru too enters suspension of payments, in 1931. Then comes the government of Sánchez Cerro, the Aprista insurrection in Trujillo in July 1932 and its repression through mass executions, the banning of APRA, the assassination of Sánchez Cerro in 1933, and the authoritarian government of Benavides until 1939 under the slogan of order, peace, and work.

It is exactly the same arc as Greece's: global economic crisis, collapse of the reformist experiment, radicalization, political violence, banning of the principal mass party, and consolidation of a conservative authoritarian regime backed by the army. And it produces the same legacy: an apparatus of surveillance and political repression against APRA that outlived Benavides and structured the relationship between the Peruvian state and the opposition for half a century.

In the rest of the world these are the years of the rise of fascism, of the Spanish Civil War, of Stalinism, of the New Deal, and of the Sino-Japanese War. The comparative conclusion matters: the crisis of interwar parliamentary democracy was not a European phenomenon but a global one, and it affected countries of the core and the periphery alike. When today's crisis of contemporary democracies is discussed, it is worth bearing in mind that there was already one, and that it was not resolved through institutional means.

sections.heading: Corfu, 1923: the dress rehearsal
paragraphs: An episode directly linked to your itinerary, one that anticipates 1940. In August 1923, the Italian general Enrico Tellini and his party, who were working on the delimitation of the Greek-Albanian border, were assassinated on Greek territory by perpetrators never identified. Mussolini sent an unacceptable ultimatum and, without waiting for a reply, BOMBED AND OCCUPIED CORFU. There were civilian deaths, including Armenian refugees housed in the old fortress.

Greece appealed to the League of Nations. Italy refused to accept its jurisdiction, and the matter was resolved at the Conference of Ambassadors, which forced Greece to pay Italy an indemnity; the Italians evacuated the island in September. In other words: the aggressor collected. It was one of the earliest demonstrations that the interwar collective security system did not work when the offender was a great power — a lesson Japan would take in Manchuria in 1931, and Italy in Ethiopia in 1935.

When you are at the old fortress of Corfu, bear in mind that it was bombed in 1923 by Italian aircraft and navy, and that it would be bombed again in 1940 and 1943. The island, neutralized by treaty in 1864 and demilitarized by the British, was attacked three times in twenty years precisely for being the gateway to the Adriatic. Neutrality decreed by others protects no one.
